activities.anchor: a transition metal is a programmable platform
activities.caption: bet on what makes the middle of the table programmable
activities.name: ccProgrammablePredict

config.q: A Group I metal does one thing enthusiastically: lose one electron. What makes a transition metal a 'programmable platform' instead?
choices: An incomplete d-subshell — variable oxidation states plus room to hold several neighbours at once
A full outer shell that resists every reaction
A heavier nucleus that forces exotic bonds
config.why: Five nearly-equal-energy d-orbitals offer the redox ladder (iron's +2 and +3, manganese's +2 to +7) and a structured embrace for ligands — the chemistry of blood, catalysts, gems and vitamin B₁₂.

activities.caption: one line of the permanganate story is wrong
activities.name: ccPermanganateSpot

config.prompt: One line of this permanganate titration summary is wrong. Find it.
lines: Acidified purple MnO₄⁻ (manganese +7) oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺
The stoichiometry is one permanganate per five irons
The manganese ends as purple Mn²⁺ in solution
Variable states also make these metals born catalysts, cycling between oxidation states
config.correction: The manganese ends as almost colourless Mn²⁺ — the purple vanishes as it falls from +7 to +2.
config.why: The colour change is the endpoint signal, and the one-per-five stoichiometry does the quantitative work; the same state-cycling is why the Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ shuttle catalyses the persulfate–iodide reaction.

config.prompt: [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ absorbs one visible frequency to hop the ligand-field split. Around what wavelength does it absorb?
config.why: Around 500 nm (green) — E = hc/λ ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 2.5 eV — so the solution transmits the complement, the red-violet lilac of titanium(III).
config.context: Change the ligands and you change the split: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ pale blue in water, deep violet in ammonia.

activities.anchor: high enough to load oxygen at lung partial pressure
activities.caption: drop the marker on the loading pressure
activities.name: ccLungPlace

config.prompt: Haemoglobin's iron binds O₂ with a stability constant tuned to load oxygen at lung partial pressure. Place the marker at that pressure:
config.why: About 21 kPa at the lung — and low enough (~4 kPa) to unload in respiring tissue; 2,3-BPG shifts the whole curve, which is why altitude acclimatisation works.

activities.anchor: Set the transition metals beside their neighbours
activities.caption: drag the divider — what the d-electrons buy
activities.name: ccGroupCompare

config.prompt: Group I vs transition metals — drag the divider:

before.label: Group I
before.text: Soft, low-density, melting near or below 100 °C; one oxidation state (+1); colourless ions; no catalysis worth the name — the single valence electron is spent on ionic bonding.

after.label: transition metals
after.text: Hard, dense, high-melting (iron 1538 °C, tungsten 3422 °C — the highest of any metal), excellent conductors, strong — d-electrons join the metallic sea, and the whole d-ladder of states is negotiable.

config.why: More shared electrons per atom means stronger metallic bonding all round — and that negotiability, not any single property, is the family's identity.
